title: Pay Attention
bodyHtml:
The meaning of a word depends on its context. For example, in the sentence “The farmer seeded the field with corn,” the word seeded means “added seeds to.” However, in the sentence “The chef seeded the tomato,” the word seeded means “took seeds away from.”

If you were building a model of language, how would you get it to to recognize the way that a word’s meaning depends on context? One popular technique for achieving this goal is a mechanism called attention. In the way that attention is implemented in current state-of-the-art models of language, the model has a large number of attention heads, each of which is denoted by a pair of numbers (for examples, 8-10). When the model processes a sentence, for every pair of words in the sentence, each head calculates the “relatedness” of the two words.

The one wrinkle is that we do not know what exactly “relatedness” should mean, so instead of telling the model how to define “relatedness,” we let the model learn its own definition of relatedness. Recently, computer scientists have started to analyze what these attention heads have learned, and this analysis shows that they often reflect linguistic information! For example, here’s the output of one attention head (head 8-10) when we feed the following sentence into BERT, which is one of the most popular models that uses attention heads:

Example: I1 see2 my3 sister4, but5 she6 can’t7 see8 me9 because10 she11 is12 reading13 a14 linguistics15 book16.

Output: 4 -> 2, 9 -> 8, 16 -> 13

This output signifies that head 8-10 connects word #4 (sister) to word #2 (see), as well as word #9 (me) to word #8 (see) and word #16 (book) to word #13 (reading). If you consider what all of those pairs of words have in common, you’ll see that each one is a verb and its direct object: sister is the direct object of the first instance of see, me is the direct object of the second instance of see, and book is the direct object of reading. It appears that head 8-10 has learn to connect verbs to their objects! (Note that these activations are directional; for example, word #2 is not connected to word #4.)

Why is this information useful? If we go back to the example with the verb seed, this sort of information can help the model figure out which version of seed is being used: If its direct object is something like field or lawn, then it probably means “to add seeds to;” if its direct object is something like tomato or watermelon, then it probably means “to take seeds away from.” Of course, one sentence isn’t enough to draw strong conclusions. Instead, computer scientists tend to use a corpus, or a database, of example sentences to find patterns in the data. Below is a small corpus, the NacloWeb Corpus, which has 7 sentences. (Some sentences derived from data in the English Web Treebank.)

NacloWeb Corpus

  1. My1 experience2 with3 Gelda4 's5 House6 of7 Gelbelgarg8 has9 been10 extremely11 wonderful12
  2. We1 use2 Google3 ‘s4 models5 to6 delve7 into8 the9 inner10 workings11 of12 language13
  3. At1 this2 corporation3 ‘s4 meeting5 people6 are7 concerned8 about9 the10 company11 's12 plans13
  4. In1 July2 we3 will4 interview5 the6 candidate7 and8 review9 her10 resumé11 again12
  5. The1 platypus2 is3 a4 strange5 animal,6 with7 its8 eggs9 and10 its11 webbed12 feet13
  6. I1 think2 that3 although4 my5 NACLO6 exam7 was8 difficult,9 it10 was11 a12 lot13 of14 fun15
  7. Linguistics1 is2 a3 beautiful4 science5 that6 provides7 interdisciplinary8 insight9 into10 the11 human12 experience13

Note that the NacloWeb corpus treats the possessive clitic ’s as a separate word. (So in Sentence #1, word #5 is ’s and word #6 is House.)

In our experiment on the NacloWeb Corpus, we ran each of the corpus’ sentences through BERT and recorded the outputs of four attention heads (8-11, 7-6, 9-6, and 5-4). Unfortunately, due to some extremely sloppy experimental procedure, we don’t remember which order we ran them through the model; in addition, we forgot to record some data. Your job is to fill in the blanks! Note that some blanks may have more than one connection, and some may have none at all.

questions.partPrompt: Identify sentences A-G: give the number (1-7) of the corpus sentence that each row of the table describes.
Fill in the missing data, labelled (a) to (i), in the table above. Write connections in the style "3 -> 4", separating several connections with a comma, or write "None".

hints.text: Start with sentence length. Every number that appears in a row must be the position of a real word in that sentence, so a row containing a large number can only belong to a long sentence. Count the words in each of the seven corpus sentences first.

Each column is one attention head doing one consistent job, the way head 8-10 in the example always linked a verb to its object. Look at the kinds of word pairs a column produces: one column links determiners (the, this, a) to the noun of their phrase, one links possessives (my, its, 's) to the word right after them, one links a preposition to the noun it takes as its object, and one links a word back to something earlier in the sentence that it refers to. Once you know what a column does, the numbers in it tell you which sentence the row must be.

Practise on the example sentence from the first page, which is not part of the table: "I(1) see(2) my(3) sister(4), but(5) she(6) can't(7) see(8) me(9) because(10) she(11) is(12) reading(13) a(14) linguistics(15) book(16)." A possessive-to-next-word head would output 3 -> 4 (my, sister); a determiner-to-noun head would output 14 -> 16 (a ... book); a refers-back head would connect she(6) or she(11) to an earlier person. Now apply the same three tests to each row of the table.

explanationHtml:
What the four columns are

An attention head is just a part of the model that, for each word, points at some other word. The example on the first page shows that head 8-10 always points from a verb's object back to the verb. The four heads in the table each have their own habit, and finding those habits is the whole puzzle.

Look at row A first. Its 9-6 cell contains the number 14, so sentence A must have at least 14 words. Only one corpus sentence is that long (the NACLO exam sentence, with 15 words), so row A is pinned down immediately. Now read that row with the sentence in front of you:

  • 8-11 gives 12 -> 13: a points at lot - a determiner pointing at its noun.
  • 7-6 gives 5 -> 6: my points at the word right after it.
  • 9-6 gives a preposition (of) pointing at a nearby noun.
  • 5-4 gives 10 -> 6: the pronoun it points back at the thing it refers to (the exam).

So, roughly: 8-11 = determiner (the, this, a) to the noun of its phrase; 7-6 = possessive (my, her, its, 's) to the following word; 9-6 = preposition to the noun it governs; 5-4 = a word pointing back at an earlier word that means the same thing (linguists call this coreference).

Using the coreference column

Column 5-4 is the most distinctive, because most sentences contain no back-reference at all. Row B has 8 -> 2 and 11 -> 2: two different words point back to the same word #2. Scan the corpus for a sentence with two possessives that refer to one earlier noun - the platypus sentence has its at #8 and its at #11, both referring to platypus at #2. Row C has 11 -> 3, and in the corporation sentence company (#11) refers back to corporation (#3). Row E has 5 -> 1, and in the linguistics sentence science (#5) is what Linguistics (#1) is.

The rows with empty 5-4 cells

Three sentences remain for rows D, F and G, and rows D and F show "None" for coreference, which fits sentences that never refer back to anything.

Row F's 7-6 cell is 1 -> 2 and 5 -> 6, so the sentence has possessives at word #1 and word #5. The Gelda's House sentence starts My experience (so 1 -> 2) and has the clitic 's as word #5 followed by House (so 5 -> 6). Its 9-6 cell, 7 -> 8, is of pointing at Gelbelgarg. That row is settled.

Row D's 7-6 cell has a single possessive at #4, and its 9-6 cell has a preposition at #12 pointing at #13. The Google models sentence has 's as word #4 before models, and of as word #12 before language. Row G, whose cells are all blank, therefore gets the one sentence left over.

Filling the blanks

Once each row has a sentence, you just apply the column's rule. For a determiner cell (8-11) list every article or demonstrative and the noun of its phrase - notice from row D that when a modifier sits in between, as in the inner workings, the head still reaches the noun. If a sentence has no article or demonstrative at all (the Gelda's House sentence has only possessives), the honest answer is "None". Likewise the possessive column is "None" for the linguistics sentence, which contains no possessive.

For row G, work through the sentence word by word: the determiner the and its noun give the 8-11 entry, the possessive her and the following word give the 7-6 entry, the opening preposition and its object give the 9-6 entry, and her pointing back to the person mentioned earlier gives the 5-4 entry.

Why the data looks slightly messy

These are real outputs from a real model, so a couple of cells are imperfect: in row E the determiner head lands on the adjective rather than the noun (a -> beautiful), and the preposition head in row B produces nothing at all. That is normal - an attention head learns a tendency, not a rule, which is exactly why researchers use a whole corpus rather than one sentence to work out what a head has learned.
_reviewNotes: Answer keys taken from the official solution page (D1: A 6, B 5, C 3, D 2, E 7, F 1, G 4; D2 (a)-(i) as printed). The booklet prints the connection symbol as a right arrow; per the ASCII-only rule for non-script symbols it is transcribed everywhere (body, prompts, answer keys) as "->". If the site's fonts do carry the arrow, a reviewer may swap "->" back to the arrow globally - do it in body, prompts, keys and variants together. No official per-part point breakdown is shown, so the 10 points are split evenly over the 16 blanks (0.625 each); adjust if a breakdown is found. No figures in this problem.
